results.key_finding: Congenital long QT syndrome (LQTS) is associated with syncope and sudden cardiac death due to Torsades de Pointes degenerating into ventricular fibrillation. LQT1 is triggered by exercise and auditory stimuli; LQT2 by auditory stimuli; LQT3 during rest or sleep. QTc ≥500 ms confers high risk. Beta-blockers are first-line therapy; ICD is recommended for high-risk patients with prior syncope or cardiac arrest.
results.title: 2022 ESC Guidelines for the Management of Patients with Ventricular Arrhythmias and the Prevention of Sudden Cardiac Death

results.key_finding: Up to 30% of patients with LQTS are initially misdiagnosed with epilepsy due to witnessed convulsive movements during syncopal episodes (convulsive syncope). Key distinguishing features include exertional or emotional triggers, absence of post-ictal confusion, brief duration, and family history of sudden cardiac death or unexplained drowning. Routine 12-lead ECG with QTc measurement is recommended in all new-onset 'seizure' evaluations.
results.title: Misdiagnosis of epilepsy in patients with channelopathies and arrhythmogenic syncope: a systematic review

results.key_finding: LQTS diagnosis requires QTc ≥480 ms on repeated ECGs, or QTc 460-480 ms in symptomatic patients. The Schwartz score integrates QTc, clinical history, family history, and symptoms. Exercise stress testing demonstrating paradoxical QTc prolongation or failure to shorten appropriately is diagnostic support for LQT1. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis (KCNQ1 mutation in LQT1). Family cascade screening is essential given autosomal dominant inheritance. Triggers in LQT1 are predominantly exercise-related.
results.source: Journal of the American College of Cardiology

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Caitlin O'Brien is a 19-year-old right-handed woman and first-year university student who is brought to the emergency department by a fellow student after collapsing during a recreational run on the campus track. She was approximately 3 km into a 5-km run at moderate pace when she suddenly went pale, dropped to the ground, and was briefly unresponsive. The witness reports that her arms and legs jerked for approximately 10 to 15 seconds. She regained consciousness within 30 seconds and was immediately alert, asking 'Did I pass out again?' She did not bite her tongue, was not incontinent, and had no confusion beyond the initial seconds. She was able to walk with assistance after two minutes.

Ms. O'Brien discloses that this is her fourth such episode in four years, all occurring during physical exertion or strong emotional arousal:
- Episode 1 (age 15): Collapsed at a swim meet shortly after completing a 200-metre freestyle event; brief convulsive movements witnessed; taken to ED, loaded with levetiracetam, discharged with a diagnosis of 'exercise-induced seizure.'
- Episode 2 (age 16): Lost consciousness during a heated argument with a sibling; jerked briefly; attributed to the prior epilepsy diagnosis; levetiracetam dose was increased.
- Episode 3 (age 17): Near-syncope during a piano recital at peak emotional excitement; managed to sit down in time and did not fully lose consciousness.
- Episode 4 (today, age 19): Collapse during running, as described.

She has been maintained on levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily since age 15 and told she has epilepsy. She attends neurology clinic annually; her last visit 8 months ago documented 'well-controlled epilepsy on medication.' She has never had a cardiac evaluation, exercise ECG, or Holter monitor. Her parents note that her maternal uncle 'drowned' at age 28 in a swimming pool with lifeguards present; no toxicology or cardiac autopsy was performed.

On direct questioning, she describes episodes as preceded by a sudden awareness that her 'heart is pounding very hard,' then light-headedness, then loss of consciousness. There is no aura, no deja vu, no olfactory changes, no automatisms, and no post-ictal confusion. She does not feel sleepy after episodes. She has noticed occasional palpitations during intense exercise over the past year that resolve spontaneously. She denies chest pain, dyspnea at rest, or leg edema. She is a non-smoker, socially active, and on no medications other than levetiracetam.

neurological_exam.additional: No tongue laceration. No lateral tongue bite. No evidence of urinary incontinence. Small bruise over left knee from fall during today's episode. No post-ictal phase — patient was fully alert and oriented within approximately 30 seconds. She reports episodes are typically preceded by brief light-headedness or 'heart pounding,' not by aura, olfactory changes, or deja vu.
